A01:2025 - Broken Access Control.description:
Access control enforces policy so that users cannot act outside their intended permissions. Failures lead to unauthorized disclosure, modification or destruction of data, or to business functions performed beyond the user's limits. Since 2025 the category also includes Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), alongside Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).

Example: An authenticated user changes the account ID in a request (GET /api/accounts/1043) and reads another customer's data.

A02:2025 - Security Misconfiguration.description:
A system, application or cloud service is set up insecurely: missing hardening, unnecessary features or accounts enabled, default credentials, overly verbose error messages, permissive cloud permissions or missing security headers. It moves up from #5 to #2 and now also covers XML External Entities (XXE).

Example: A production server keeps the debug console and the default admin account enabled, and shows stack traces to users.

A03:2025 - Software Supply Chain Failure.description:
Breakdowns or compromises in building, distributing or updating software: vulnerable, unmaintained or untracked components, malicious dependencies, insecure CI/CD pipelines. It extends the former “Vulnerable and Outdated Components” to the whole supply chain and has the highest average exploit and impact scores in the 2025 data.

Example: The application ships a JavaScript library with a known CVE, and the build pipeline pulls dependencies without pinning versions or verifying signatures.

A04:2025 - Cryptographic Failures.description:
Failures related to missing or weak cryptography: data sent or stored in cleartext, obsolete algorithms or protocols, poor key management, unvalidated certificates, weak randomness. They expose sensitive data in transit and at rest.

Example: Passwords stored as unsalted MD5 hashes, or session tokens generated with a non-cryptographic random number generator.

A05:2025 - Injection.description:
Untrusted input reaches an interpreter (browser, database, shell, LDAP, template engine) and is executed as part of a command or query. It includes Cross-Site Scripting, very frequent, and SQL injection, less frequent but with high impact.

Example: A login form vulnerable to SQL injection: the input ' OR '1'='1 grants access without valid credentials.

A06:2025 - Insecure Design.description:
Security controls that are missing or ineffective by design, including flaws in business logic. A perfect implementation cannot fix an insecure design: it takes threat modeling, secure design patterns and reference architectures.

Example: A checkout flow lets the client set the item price, or password recovery relies on security questions whose answers are public.

A07:2025 - Authentication Failures.description:
The system can be tricked into accepting an invalid user as legitimate: credential stuffing and brute force not blocked, default or weak passwords, weak recovery flows, missing or bypassable MFA, session identifiers that are not rotated or invalidated.

Example: The session ID is not regenerated after login, enabling session fixation.

A08:2025 - Software or Data Integrity Fa.description:
Code or data from untrusted sources is treated as trusted without verifying its integrity: unsigned updates, plugins or CDN resources, insecure deserialization, object attributes changed by the client (mass assignment).

Example: The application deserializes a cookie value without verifying its signature, and the attacker gets remote code execution.

A09:2025 - Security Logging & Alerting F.description:
Without logging, monitoring and alerting, attacks and breaches go undetected and the response comes late. It covers unlogged security events, logs without integrity protection, sensitive data written to logs, and alerting thresholds that are missing or ignored.

Example: A brute-force attack goes unnoticed because failed logins are neither logged nor alerted on.

A10:2025 - Mishandling of Exceptional Co.description:
New in 2025: the application fails to prevent, detect or handle abnormal conditions. Unhandled exceptions, error messages that leak internal details and logic that fails open lead to crashes, inconsistent states and bypassed controls.

Example: An exception in the authorization check is caught by a generic handler that lets the request through (fail open).
